newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FEATURE-Australian wool warms to price surge.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Australian wool warms to price surge.

text.p: GEELONG, Australia, June 3 (Reuter)
- A recent surge in Australian wool prices has brought with it a turnaround in sentiment for the country's A$2.5 billion wool export industry.
A two-day meeting here at the close of last week of the Wool Council of Australia (WCA) coincided with the rise of local wool auction prices to the 700 cents/kg mark, a 21-month high.
And with that good news, the industry's attentions visibly switched from divisive political battles to common strategies on how best to capitalise from the price rise.
Once one of Australia's premier industries - in decades past the entire country was said to "ride on the sheep's back" - wool has been given the chance to rise again.
"A gap is emerging between demand and supply and it is important for Australia to fill the gap," Alec Morrison, chairman of the International Wool Secretariat (IWS), said.
"No other country can fill it. It's an opportunity for Australia," he said.
A FINE LINE FOR WOOL

But wool is nevertheless balanced on a very fine line. Increasing supply is seen as both a challenge and a threat. Even as prices rise, farmers remember the devastation in the industry's production base caused by the collapse of prices to a low of 388 cents/kg in 1992 from a peak of 1,269 cents in 1988.

Nobody knows exactly how many wool growers have left the industry in recent years, but WCA president Rod Thirkell-Johnston estimates the number at about 70,000, leaving about 50,000 growers. About one-fifth of these are major producers.

The number of sheep in Australia also needs to be re-built, with the present sheep population of about 122 million projected to rise to about 136 million by year 2000. At its peak in 1990, the flock numbered 173 million. With present world demand for merino fleece seen as 20 percent greater than Australia can produce, the gap is currently filled by sales of a minimum of 135,000 bales a quarter from Australia's 1.7 million bale stockpile. Australia is the world's leading producer of fine merino fleece.

The stockpile, being steadily sold down from its peak of 4.72 million bales in February 1991, set as the old floor price scheme collapsed, is to be completely sold out by 2000. Australia's need to increase wool supply is countered by fear of the over-production trap which caused the last collapse in prices and the rise of the stockpile mountain.

Morrison believes wool will begin to lose market share in its battle with synthetics and other fibres at prices of between 800 cents and 1,000 cents/kg. Wool's current price ratio to synthetics is already seen as high.
CAUGHT IN THE CROSSFIRE
The central point to emerge from this year's conference was well made by Bob Richardson, chief executive of Wool International, the statutory body charge of stockpile sales.

Richards said current prices presented something of a dilemma for the wool industry. "It is caught in the crossfire between a price too high to gain market share in a competitive low-growth fibre market and too low to stimulate some shift of resources from cropping back to grazing that may be required in three years when the stockpile is gone," he said.
Richardson described wool's price rise as possibly too quick. "It remains to be seen how durable the recent price rises will be," he said.
Macquarie Bank, the leading financial player in developing wool price hedging instruments, was optimistic this week on the development of its risk management tools.

Randell Heyman, director of treasury and commodities at the Macquarie Bank, said the bank's forward micron indicator cash-settled hedge market had grown considerably in the past six months. Trading in growers' tax entitlements to stockpile wool was also expected to expand when trading begins, he said. Heyman's point that volatility helped those who used risk management tools wisely, as wool faces its new price surge, was well received by this week's conference.
Heyman said Macquarie believed price volatility was here to stay and would increase as the Australian stockpile was cut.
"But volatility helps to make money," he added.
